> This ESP32 TFT display Project is a piece of embedded hardware that contains a touch screen, display and audio output. The main part of the device is the ESP32 microcontroller. The ESP32 communicates with the 2.8" ILI9341 SPI TFT display allowing visual output. Inputs are provided by the physical buttons and touch screen. Audio is provided by the ESP32 reading audio files from the internal flash memory (using the littleFS file system) and sending the audio signal to the ESP32’s DAC. The signal is amplified by the onboard PAM8302 Class-D mono amplifier to power the external 8 Ohm mini speaker. The traces have been routed carefully so that there are no issues with digital signal interference with the audio signals. This device has been created on a bespoke 71x71mm PCB created using JLCPCB.

## Design

### 2026-11-01: I worked on it a little bit (6 hours from 12 - 6)  yesterday, and immediately after I went to bowl and then trick or treat with my friends so I didn't get to log the hours but I did keep a journal of

**15h**

I worked on it a little bit (6 hours from 12 - 6)  yesterday, and immediately after I went to bowl and then trick or treat with my friends so I didn't get to log the hours but I did keep a journal of it and this took  me a very loooooong time so heres my journal:

First step was to visit the esp32 website to understand how best to name my nets. I did some targeted research into the ESP32's pinout restrictions to ensure that hardware SPI and touch lines were not allocated to the boot-strapping pins which would cause the microcontroller to lock up. Studied the communications protocol and 3.3v logic level requirements of the 2.8" ILI9341 SPI TFT display to ensure it would work with the TFT_eSPI libraries. Looked into audio options to play sounds so decided to use the PAM8302 class-D amplifier to amplify the ESP32 DAC signal to the small 8 Ohm external speaker. The analog audio signal was separated from any digital interference. Looked into audio storage options. Decided between using the internal flash memory with the LittleFS system or using an external SPI microSD card. Reviewed JLCPCB's manufacture guidelines. Learned that CPL position files require the Designator column header. Also learned that Standard PCBA requires 5mm edge rails.

![Schematic image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/aognY8UOVQB9hZBPwkQkR9oFPOAPqNn0/f93424e88a82dbb043cc6cbc153b326a35355d740751819ee2a55cfb2d7c5c2d.png)

Once this was done, I designed the entire schematic in KiCad connecting the ESP32 module to the 2.8inch ILI9341 TFT Display using SPI serial communication, along with push button switches, pin headers, resistors and decoupling capacitors.

I then performed a Design Rule Check (DRC). I received some errors such as floating net flags on the display header pins, trace clearance issues around the ground pin on the ESP32 Module, and an un-routed airwire on the 3.3V power rail. Once I fixed these issues, the DRC passed without any errors. I then created my Gerber and BOM files.

When exporting my CPL file for positioning I ran into an issue with JLCPCB where it would not accept my file due to an error with the file. To fix this I opened my CSV file in Notepad and renamed the first column title from Ref to Designator. Due to the ESP32 Module footprint I had to change my assembly service to Standard PCBA, meaning I added 5mm edges to my board making the board 71mm x 71mm.

Looking at the 3D preview on JLCPCB I noticed that components such as headers and buttons did not look right and were not positioned correctly. However, checking my design with the 3D Viewer tool in KiCad I can see everything is correct. This shows that the pick and place machines only use co-ordinates from the CPL file.

Trying to place my order I received an error about caching. The error said that Standard PCBA does not support nitrogen reflow. To fix this I toggled the option to ‘Yes’ then back to ‘No’. I then changed the product description to Electronic Board / Parts and saved my order to my basket. I also double checked that the DIANN 2.8inch 320x240 ILI9341 SPI TFT Display Module was fully compatible with my PCB Headers and 3.3v/5v logic. Due to my tight deadline of 2.5hours I chose to go with JLCPCB rather than wait for the manual engineering process with PCBWay.
(I actually did another 3 hours ill add that in the next one).
